hikes.name: Rider Canyon

hikes.name: North Canyon
hikes.desc: Narrowing red Supai slot to a still reflecting pool under polished walls; perfect early leg-stretch. The first "classic" hike in the canyon. If the creek is running, there's potential for fun waterslides connecting the pools in the narrows.

hikes.name: Silver Grotto

hikes.name: South Canyon / Stanton's Cave
hikes.desc: Easy at the bottom. Difficult, steep climb through the Redwall and eventually to the rim. Might be possible to reach the (now gated shut) Stanton's Cave

hikes.name: Nautiloid Canyon
hikes.desc: Easy walk up a bed of fossil nautiloids; splash the rock to make them pop.

hikes.name: Buck Farm Canyon
hikes.desc: Giant Redwall faces and springs that support ferns.

hikes.name: Eminence Break
hikes.desc: Good hike to the rim on a layover day or a shorter hike to a nice view at the top of the Redwall.

hikes.name: Saddle Canyon
hikes.desc: Shady creek-bed with a steep gully and boulder-hopping to a fern-draped waterfall and narrows.

hikes.name: 50-Mile Diving Board
hikes.desc: Steep, exposed scrambling, and difficult but very rewarding

hikes.name: Nankoweap Canyon
hikes.desc: Longer wander up the delta and drainage below the granaries; big open camp with room to roam.

hikes.name: Nankoweap Granaries
hikes.desc: Steep, exposed climb to cliff granaries ~700 ft above the river - the most photographed view on the river. The 'Canyon Stairmaster.'

hikes.name: Kwagunt Creek
hikes.desc: Sister creek to Nankoweap. Good alternative to the more popular sibling.

hikes.name: Little Colorado Confluence
hikes.desc: Turquoise travertine water for swimming/chutes (when not flooding); sacred Hopi/Zuni site - tread lightly.

hikes.name: Walter Powell Route

hikes.name: Carbon-Chuar Loop

hikes.name: Carbon-Lava Loop

hikes.name: Tanner Trail

hikes.name: The Tabernacle

hikes.name: Clear Creek

hikes.name: Monument Creek

hikes.name: Hermit Creek

hikes.name: Elves Chasm

geology.d: At Lees Ferry the river starts on the Moenkopi — chocolate-brown mudstones and ripple-marked siltstones, the youngest rock the river touches. About 245 million years ago, in the Early Triassic, this was a vast, nearly flat coastal plain on the western shore of the supercontinent Pangaea, sitting just above sea level near 10°N — hot and seasonally wet, crossed by sluggish rivers and washed by shallow tides that left the ripple marks and mud cracks. Life was only just recovering from the largest mass extinction in Earth's history a few million years before; the mudflats held amphibians and early reptiles whose tracks survive, in a world still millions of years shy of the first dinosaurs.

The gray, fossil-rich limestone that caps both rims meets the water as you enter Marble Canyon. Around 270 million years ago this whole region lay beneath a warm, shallow tropical sea — Arizona was underwater on a broad marine shelf near the equator, at the western edge of Pangaea. The clear, sunlit water teemed with brachiopods, crinoids (sea lilies), bryozoans, corals, mollusks, and sponges, whose glassy spicules formed the chert nodules scattered through the rock. Sharks cruised the shelf, and their teeth still turn up in the Kaibab.

A slope-forming mix of limestone, sandstone, and gypsum, exposed only briefly in upper Marble Canyon. About 273 million years ago the Permian shoreline swung back and forth across this spot: at times a shallow sea full of brachiopods and mollusks, at times a hot, restricted lagoon and sabkha flat where seawater evaporated to leave gypsum, and at times a coastal dune field. The climate was arid and tropical and the region still near the equator — a landscape of salt flats and salty embayments alternating with open marine water.

Cream-colored, cross-bedded sandstone — the petrified dunes of an enormous desert. Around 275 million years ago this was a sand sea the size of the modern Sahara, a bone-dry erg of wind-driven dunes stretched across equatorial Pangaea. There was no sea here at all; the sweeping cross-beds record the slip-faces of migrating dunes. Almost nothing lived on the open sand, but its damp margins preserve delicate trackways — the footprints of early reptiles and the trails of scorpions, spiders, and millipedes climbing the dunes.

Deep-red mudstones and siltstones — the red that begins to color the river corridor. About 280 million years ago this was a low, muddy coastal floodplain near sea level, crossed by slow, meandering rivers; the iron in its muds rusted red in a seasonally dry, oxidizing climate, and preserved frost cracks hint at cool winters. Unlike the barren desert above it, the Hermit floodplain was green: ferns, seed ferns, and early conifers grew along the streams, and the rock preserves their leaves along with insect wings and the tracks of amphibians and reptiles.

The uppermost formation of the Supai Group — a resistant, dark-red sandstone that forms the prominent Esplanade bench about a quarter of the way down the canyon, creating its "canyon within a canyon" profile. Around 290 million years ago wind-driven coastal dunes marched along the western edge of Pangaea near the equator; the sweeping cross-beds are their fossilized slip-faces. It is the time-equivalent of Utah's Cedar Mesa Sandstone (Cutler Group), and cyanobacteria, lichens, and mosses still cling to its surface today.

The second formation down in the Supai Group, a Late Pennsylvanian red sequence of sandstone and mudstone about 300 million years old. It records a low coastal plain crossed by rivers and fringed by dunes near the equator, laid down as sea level rose and fell with distant ice ages at Pangaea's far south pole. An erosional surface caps it, where the land stood briefly above the sea before the Esplanade dunes buried it.

The third formation of the Supai Group, roughly 305 million years old. Its interbedded red sandstones and thin limestones record a shifting equatorial shoreline — dunes and river flats alternating with shallow, briny seas as ice-age sea levels pulsed up and down. Marine layers hold brachiopods and other sea life; sandy layers preserve the tracks of amphibians and early reptiles.

The bottom formation of the Supai Group, about 315 million years old, resting on the Redwall below. Grayer and more marine than the red beds above it, it formed on a shallow tropical sea floor and coastal flats, its limestones full of brachiopods, crinoids, and other marine life. It marks the base of the roughly 30-million-year Supai story.

The canyon's great gray cliff-former, stained red by iron washing down from the Supai above; Redwall Cavern at Mile 33 is carved into it. Around 340 million years ago Arizona lay under a clear, warm, shallow tropical sea right at the equator — a vast carbonate platform. It was one of the richest marine scenes in the canyon's whole story: meadows of crinoids (sea lilies) swayed in the current alongside corals, brachiopods, and bryozoans, and straight-shelled nautiloids — cone-shaped cephalopods — crowd Nautiloid Canyon. Sharks and fish patrolled the warm water above.

Purple-gray dolomite and limestone that fills ancient tidal channels carved into the Muav below — the only Devonian rock in the canyon, about 385 million years old. It settled across a 120-million-year gap in the record, in shallow seas and tidal channels during the 'Age of Fishes,' when armored placoderms and other early fish swam warm equatorial water. It stands on its own, belonging to no group.

The gray, cliff-and-ledge limestone that sculpts the 'Muav Gorge' — the youngest of the three Tonto Group formations. About 505 million years ago it was lime mud settling offshore in the same warm, shallow Cambrian sea that laid the Bright Angel and Tapeats beneath it, the region underwater near the equator. Trilobites and brachiopods lived on and in the seafloor.

Green and maroon marine shale, the soft middle formation of the Tonto Group that erodes into the broad Tonto Platform. About 505 million years ago the Cambrian sea had deepened over this spot, and Arizona lay underwater on a muddy offshore shelf below wave base; the green mineral glauconite confirms its marine birth. This was the world of the Cambrian Explosion — trilobites crawled and swam in abundance, brachiopods clustered on the seafloor, and worm-like animals left a lacework of burrows — while the land above the waves was still utterly barren rock, long before plants or animals colonized it.

Dark, slabby, cliff-forming sandstone — the basal formation of the Tonto Group, whose own base is the Great Unconformity, a gap of more than a billion years. Around 510–520 million years ago this was a beach and shallow tidal shoreline, the leading edge of the very first sea to flood across the long-eroded ancient landscape, its cross-bedded sands recording tidal channels and surf. Trilobites plowed the sandy bottom, leaving distinctive trackways alongside brachiopods and other early animals — while the adjacent land was still bare stone, since nothing yet lived out of the water.

Dark lava flows that cap the Unkar Group, erupted about 1.1 billion years ago as the crust stretched and began to rift apart; molten basalt spread over the Dox mudflats below. It is the youngest unit of the tilted Unkar Group — the lowest of the three subdivisions of the Grand Canyon Supergroup (the Nankoweap Formation and the Chuar Group once lay above it, mostly eroded away here). Earth held only single-celled, microbial life.

A thick, slope-forming sequence of red and purple mudstone and sandstone — the most voluminous formation of the Unkar Group, about 1.19 billion years old. It accumulated on a broad tidal flat and river delta, its surfaces printed with mud cracks, ripple marks, and salt-crystal casts. Mats of cyanobacteria were the only life in this Precambrian world.

A hard, cliff-forming red-purple quartzite of the Unkar Group, roughly 1.2 billion years old, made from beach and delta sands later cemented to stone. It was tough enough that hills of it stood as islands in the Cambrian Tapeats sea half a billion years later, poking up through the younger sandstone.

Brilliant orange and red shale and sandstone of the Unkar Group, about 1.2 billion years old, whose vivid color lights up the Unkar area. It formed on tidal flats and a shallow shelf, with mud cracks recording the times those flats dried out. Only microbial mats lived here.

The bottom formation of the Unkar Group and the oldest of the Grand Canyon Supergroup here — a gray dolomitic limestone about 1.25 billion years old, resting on the ancient Vishnu basement. It formed in a shallow sea, and its layered stromatolites — mounds built by mats of cyanobacteria — are the clearest fossils of that microbial world, in a time with no animals and no plants at all.

geology.full: Vishnu Basement Rocks — Upper Granite Gorge
geology.d: At Hance the river drops into black, glittering Vishnu Schist laced with pink Zoroaster Granite — 1.7-billion-year-old roots of a lost mountain range and the oldest rock you'll touch. It began as volcanic islands and seafloor sediments in an ancient ocean, then, as early continents collided, was buried some twelve miles deep and cooked and squeezed into schist while molten granite injected through it — building a Himalaya-scale range now eroded to its very roots. This is the Upper Granite Gorge: Sockdolager, Granite, Hermit, and Crystal. Earth had oxygen by then, but life was still nothing more than single cells in the sea.

Below the Upper Granite Gorge the ancient Vishnu dives away and the Cambrian Tonto Group — Tapeats Sandstone and Bright Angel Shale — returns to river level, opening the canyon out again. These are the same roughly 505–520-million-year-old deposits seen upstream: the beach sands and offshore muds of the first sea to drown this coast, when trilobites ruled a shallow seafloor beneath an otherwise lifeless landscape.

geology.full: Vishnu Basement Rocks — Middle Granite Gorge
geology.d: The 1.7-billion-year-old schist and granite rise back to the water for a short, dark inner canyon — the Middle Granite Gorge, around Bedrock and Deubendorf. Like the Upper Gorge, this is metamorphic rock born miles deep in the crust during an ancient mountain-building collision, from a time when only microbes lived in Earth's oceans and the continents were bare stone — the oldest, most deeply buried rock briefly returning to the surface.

Through the open middle canyon the river runs mostly on the Cambrian Tonto Group and Muav Limestone, with the Redwall and Supai stepping back up the walls; near Havasu (Mile 157) the water polishes gray Muav. These rocks record warm, shallow tropical seas that repeatedly flooded the region between about 505 and 340 million years ago — first the Cambrian sea of trilobites and brachiopods, later the crinoid-rich carbonate seas of the Mississippian — all while this part of Arizona sat underwater near the equator. (Reach boundaries here are approximate.)

geology.age: erupted within the last ~1 million years
geology.d: Here two wildly different ages meet. The bedrock is Paleozoic marine limestone — old tropical seafloor — but the reach is defined by something startlingly young: black basalt from volcanoes on the north rim that erupted directly into the already-carved canyon within roughly the last million years, much of it within the last few hundred thousand. Molten lava poured over the rim and repeatedly dammed the Colorado, backing up lakes that then failed catastrophically; Lava Falls (Mile 179) sits amid that debris. When these eruptions lit the canyon, Ice Age Arizona was cooler and greener, roamed by mammoths, ground sloths, and other megafauna. (Approximate reach.)

geology.full: Vishnu Basement Rocks — Lower Granite Gorge
geology.d: Below Diamond Creek the river enters its last dark inner canyon, the Lower Granite Gorge, cutting once more into 1.7-billion-year-old Vishnu schist and granite. As in the gorges upstream, this is the deeply buried, metamorphosed root of an ancient mountain range — from a time when the seas held only single-celled life and the continents were bare. (Approximate reach.)

Approaching Pearce Ferry the strata rise and the walls step back down through Paleozoic marine limestones and sandstones — the same ancient tropical-sea rocks, here lifted along the Grand Wash Fault. That fault is the sharp western edge of the Colorado Plateau, where it drops into the stretched, faulted Basin and Range that began pulling apart around 15 million years ago; the Grand Wash Cliffs mark the very end of the Grand Canyon. Today the moving river gives way here to the still water of Lake Mead, a reservoir less than a century old.

items.d: Small gray toad flecked with orange-red warts; its long, high, musical trill fills the canyon on warm nights after rain.
A large toad with a pale mid-back stripe; gives a nasal, sheep-like 'waaah' from river backwaters and pools.
A soft-spoken toad of clear rocky streams and springs, now scarce where it hybridizes with Woodhouse's Toad.
Named for the black 'spade' on each hind foot used to dig backward into soil; emerges explosively to breed in rain pools.
A warty, rock-colored treefrog that basks on boulders by day; its loud, resonant call echoes off canyon walls at dusk.
A green, spotted native frog of desert springs and streams, much reduced by drying and invasive bullfrogs.
The largest North American frog and an aggressive invader that eats native frogs, fish, and hatchling turtles wherever it spreads.
A stout, blotched salamander that spends most of its life underground, appearing at pools and tanks only to breed.
Familiar honking goose; pairs and family groups graze sandbars and loaf on quiet river eddies.
A subtly handsome gray dabbling duck; the drake shows a black stern and a chestnut wing patch in flight.
A whistling dabbler; the drake's white crown earned it the old name 'baldpate.'
The classic green-headed duck, ancestor of most domestic ducks; dabbles in shallows and backwaters.
A small duck; the breeding drake is a striking rich cinnamon-red with a ruby eye.
An elegant, long-necked dabbler; the drake's namesake needle-thin tail points skyward.
North America's smallest dabbling duck, fast and agile, twisting in tight flocks over the water.
A diving duck with a round rufous head and gray body; winters on open river reaches.
A tiny, bold black-and-white diver; the drake wears a big white 'bonnet' and nests in old flicker holes.
A compact diver with a bright golden eye and round white cheek spot; its wings whistle in flight.
A large, sleek, fish-eating duck with a saw-edged bill; cruises the current and dives for fish.
A plump desert quail with a teardrop head plume; coveys scurry through brush giving a bright 'chi-ca-go-go' call.
A stocky partridge of rocky slopes introduced from Eurasia, with barred flanks and a bold black necklace; prized by hunters, hard to catch.
Large native game bird of the rim forests; the local Merriam's form has pale tail tips and occasionally wanders lower.
A small brown diving bird that sinks quietly out of sight; its ringed bill and pumping call give it away.
An elegant black-and-white diver with a swan-like neck, famed for its dancing courtship 'rush' across the water.
The city pigeon, introduced from Europe; nests on cliff ledges just as its wild ancestors did.
A pale dove with a black neck-ring; a rapid Old World colonizer now widespread across the West.
A desert dove with bold white wing-stripes; its 'who-cooks-for-you' cooing is a sound of summer, and it feeds on cactus fruit.
Slim, fast, and abundant; its mournful cooing and whistling wingbeats are everywhere in the Southwest.
A slim, secretive riparian bird called the 'rain crow' for calling on humid days; a threatened cottonwood-willow specialist.
An iconic ground-running cuckoo that sprints after lizards and snakes; woven into many Southwestern legends as clever and lucky.
A moth-like dusk flier that courses low over the river for insects; roosts invisibly on the ground by day.
A small nightjar that calls its name from rocky slopes; the only bird known to truly hibernate, which the Hopi noted long ago.
A cigar-shaped rocket of the cliffs, among the fastest birds in level flight; nests deep in canyon crevices.
The common breeding hummingbird of the corridor; the male's black chin flashes violet in good light.
A hardy hummingbird with a rose-red crown and throat; the male dives with an explosive squeak.
A desert hummingbird; the male's brilliant purple gorget flares out like a mustache.
A mountain hummingbird whose male makes a loud metallic wing-trill in flight; visits the canyon in migration.
A feisty coppery migrant that passes through in numbers, fueling on wildflowers along the way.
A slate-gray waterbird with a white bill and big lobed toes; dives and dabbles in quiet backwaters.
A noisy shorebird of gravel bars that feigns a broken wing to lure predators away from its nest.
A small sandpiper that teeters constantly and flies on stiff, fluttering wingbeats low over the water; females hold the territory.
A tidy medium gull with a black-ringed bill; follows rivers and reservoirs, especially in winter.
A dark, long-necked diver that swims low and perches with wings spread to dry; hunts fish underwater.
A tall, patient stalker of the shallows that spears fish with a lightning strike; often stands statue-still on the bank.
A stately all-white heron with a yellow dagger bill; its plumes were once hunted nearly to extinction for hats.
A dainty white egret with 'golden slippers' — black legs and bright yellow feet it shuffles to stir up prey.
A teetering soarer with a bare red head that finds carrion by smell, a rare talent among birds; a summer resident.
North America's largest land bird, back from the brink of extinction and reintroduced at nearby Vermilion Cliffs in 1996; each wears numbered wing tags, so report sightings.
The 'fish hawk' that hovers then plunges talons-first for fish; migrates along the river.
The national bird; winters along the river to fish and scavenge where trout gather, and is sacred to many Native nations.
A low-coursing hawk with a white rump and owl-like face; quarters flats hunting partly by sound.
A small, dashing forest hawk that ambushes songbirds; migrates through the canyon in numbers.
A crow-sized bird-hunting hawk with a long banded tail; threads through trees after doves and quail.
A black hawk that mimics a Turkey Vulture, tilting among them to surprise the prey below.
The West's most familiar hawk; its rusty tail and screaming call are a canyon staple — that scream is the 'eagle' cry in most movies.
A powerful cliff-nesting eagle that takes rabbits and even young bighorn; its feathers are deeply sacred to many tribes.
A ghostly, heart-faced owl that hunts rodents by sound in total darkness; gives an eerie raspy shriek.
A small eared owl of riparian trees that sings a bouncing-ball series of whistles at night.
The canyon's apex nocturnal hunter, with ear tufts and deep hooting; takes prey up to skunks and other owls.
A threatened, dark-eyed owl of shady side canyons; roosts in cool, narrow slots by day.
A big-headed, rattling bird that hovers then dives for fish; both sexes dig nest burrows in riverbanks.
Drills neat rows of 'wells' in bark and returns to sip the sap and trapped insects; a winter visitor.
A small black-and-white desert woodpecker with a ladder back; taps at cactus, agave, and mesquite.
The smallest North American woodpecker; forages on riparian trees and stems, often near cottonwoods.
A large brown woodpecker that feeds on the ground for ants; western birds flash salmon-red under the wings.
A jay-sized, colorful falcon that hovers over open ground for insects and mice; our smallest falcon.
A small, fierce, fast falcon that runs down songbirds in flight; a winter visitor.
A pale desert falcon of open cliffs; a low, fast hunter of ground squirrels and birds.
The fastest animal alive, diving over 200 mph; the Grand Canyon holds one of the densest nesting populations anywhere.
A drab flycatcher that sallies from a snag; its burry, descending call is a summer sound of the corridor.
A plain 'empid' flycatcher; the Southwestern subspecies is federally endangered and nests in dense riverside willows and tamarisk.
A crisp black-and-white flycatcher that pumps its tail from streamside perches; never far from water.
A soft apricot-bellied flycatcher of open ground; often the most-seen bird along the river banks.
The male is a startling flame-red; flutters and hovers in courtship over green riverside spots.
A pale desert flycatcher that nests in cavities and feeds on insects and even small lizards in dry washes.
A larger, loud summer flycatcher of tall riparian trees; gives a sharp 'whit' call.
A gray-and-yellow flycatcher that fearlessly chases off hawks and ravens; perches on open snags.
A plain, restless vireo of dense willow thickets that sings a rushed, scolding song and nests along the river.
A gray vireo with bold 'spectacles'; a deliberate forager of pinyon-juniper and canyon trees.
A drab but sweet-voiced vireo whose warbling song drifts from cottonwood canopies in migration.
A social blue jay of pinyon-juniper that caches thousands of pine seeds; roving flocks effectively plant future forests.
A dark, crested jay of the higher rims and side canyons; bold, loud, and a skilled mimic.
A crestless blue-and-gray jay of pinyon-juniper that caches acorns and pine nuts.
A familiar all-black corvid, smaller than a raven with a fan-shaped tail; social and clever.
The canyon's ever-present acrobat and problem-solver, a trickster and creator figure across many Native traditions; will raid unguarded camp food.
A tiny, tame bird with a white eyebrow; whistles 'cheeseburger' from higher conifers and side canyons.
A plain gray crested bird of pinyon-juniper that scolds boldly and hammers open seeds.
A tiny gray desert bird with a yellow head; builds conspicuous ball-shaped nests in thorny shrubs.
A minute, long-tailed gray bird that travels in busy flocks and weaves a remarkable hanging sock-nest.
A ground bird of open flats with tiny black 'horns' and a face mask; runs rather than hops.
A plain brown swallow that nests in riverbank burrows and skims insects over the water.
A small colonial swallow with a brown breast-band that digs nest tunnels in cutbanks.
A jewel-toned swallow of the cliffs, green above and violet-rumped, flashing white on the face.
Builds gourd-shaped mud nests in colonies under overhangs and bridges; wheels over the river in tight flocks.
The classic long-tailed, orange-bellied swallow; builds cup nests on ledges and courses low over the water.
A tiny, hyperactive olive bird that flicks its wings; the male hides a scarlet crown patch. A winter visitor.
A stubby bird that creeps head-first down trunks, giving a nasal 'yank-yank' in riparian and pine woods.
A pale wren of talus and boulders that bobs constantly and paves its nest entrance with tiny stones.
A rusty cliff wren whose cascading, silvery song spilling down the rock is the definitive sound of the Grand Canyon.
A small, energetic brown wren with a bubbling song; nests in cavities in riparian woods.
A long-tailed wren with a white eyebrow it flicks side to side; a varied, musical singer.
The Southwest's big, boisterous wren; builds football-sized nests in cholla and gives a low, chugging call.
A secretive wren of cattails and reeds; the male builds many dummy nests and sings a reedy rattle.
A tiny, slender blue-gray bird with a long white-edged tail it flicks while gleaning insects.
A desert gnatcatcher of dry washes, mostly black under the tail, giving a rasping call year-round.
A stout gray songbird that walks underwater in rushing streams to feed and bobs endlessly on midstream rocks; look for it on clear tributaries.
A deep-blue thrush with a rusty breast that drops from perches to snap up insects in open woods.
A shy brown thrush with a reddish tail; its flute-like song is among the most beautiful in North America. A winter visitor.
The familiar orange-breasted thrush; gathers at berries and damp ground, common in winter flocks.
A gray mimic that strings together the songs of dozens of other birds, singing day and night.
A secretive, long-billed thrasher of dense desert thickets, rusty under the tail and heard more than seen.
A small, streaky thrasher of sagebrush flats; a rich, tireless singer in migration.
A glossy, speckled invader introduced to New York in the 1890s; competes aggressively with native cavity-nesters.
A slim, glossy-black crested bird with red eyes that eats mistletoe berries and spreads the plant — the two depend on each other.
A sleek, crested bird with waxy red wingtips; roving winter flocks strip berries from riparian trees.
A chunky sparrow brought from Europe and tied to human settlement, now found near people worldwide.
A slim ground bird of open shores that walks (not hops) and wags its tail; a winter and migration visitor to gravel bars.
A cheerful red-fronted finch of dry country and towns; the male's red color comes from his diet.
A raspberry-tinged finch of higher conifer forests that wanders down in winter.
A small, streaky, sharp-billed finch with yellow wing flashes; nomadic winter flocks descend on seeds.
A tiny black-and-gold finch with a sweet, wandering song; feeds on thistle and weed seeds.
A large sparrow with a rufous cap and greenish tail that scratches in brush and mews like a cat.
A boldly patterned towhee with red eyes and white-spotted wings that rummages loudly in leaf litter.
A plain brown towhee with a black face, endemic to Southwestern riparian thickets; stays low in dense cover.
A small, clean sparrow with a rusty cap and crisp face lines; trills from open woodland edges.
A plain, finely streaked sparrow of sagebrush that delivers a surprisingly long, buzzy, canary-like song.
A crisp desert sparrow with a black bib and bold white face stripes; thrives on the driest, rockiest ground.
A large sparrow with a harlequin chestnut-and-white head pattern; forages on open ground.
A tidy gray-and-white sparrow that flashes white outer tail feathers; abundant in winter flocks, with several regional forms.
A handsome sparrow with bold black-and-white head stripes and a clear whistled song; common in winter brush.
A streaky, versatile sparrow of streamside brush that sings a bright, variable song nearly year-round.
A streaky sparrow with white outer tail feathers and a white eye-ring that sings most sweetly at dusk.
An oversized, skulking 'warbler' with a brilliant yellow breast and a bizarre medley of whistles, chuckles, and rattles from dense willows.
The male flashes red-and-yellow shoulders and sings 'conk-la-ree' from cattails and reeds.
A brood parasite that lays its eggs in other birds' nests; it followed bison herds historically, and cattle today.
A big, glossy blackbird with a keel-shaped tail and loud, clanking calls; expanding across the Southwest.
A sleek blackbird; the male gleams purple-and-green with a pale eye and forages boldly on open ground.
A flame-orange-and-black oriole that weaves a hanging pouch nest in cottonwoods; a signature summer bird of the corridor.
A slender orange oriole that stitches its nest to the underside of palm and cottonwood leaves; a summer visitor.
A plain olive warbler with a rarely-seen orange crown that forages low in brush during migration.
A tiny gray desert warbler with a rusty rump — one of only two cavity-nesting warblers, and the most abundant breeding bird along the river.
A masked, wren-like warbler of marshy edges; the male sings a rolling 'witchety-witchety' from the reeds.
A sweet-singing, all-yellow warbler of willows; the male is streaked chestnut below. A classic riverside breeder.
The hardy, adaptable warbler with a signal-yellow rump; by far the most common wintering warbler.
A crisp black-white-and-gray warbler with a tiny yellow spot before the eye; a migrant through pinyon-juniper.
A skulking warbler with a gray hood and white eye-arcs that stays low in streamside tangles during migration.
A bright yellow warbler; the male wears a neat black cap. An active, tail-flicking migrant in the willows.
The male is entirely rose-red — a bee and wasp specialist that catches them in midair; a prized riparian breeder.
A flame-headed, yellow-and-black bird that seems tropical; passes through canyon trees in migration.
A robin-sized bird with a heavy seed-cracking bill; the male is burnt-orange and black with a rich warbling song.
A deep-blue bird with chestnut wingbars and a big silver bill that sings from riverside shrubs in summer.
A small finch-like bird; the male is turquoise-blue with a cinnamon breast, singing from open brush.
An endangered fish found only in the Colorado River basin; its odd fleshy hump and huge fins help it hold position in fierce whitewater.
A small, hardy native minnow of streams and shorelines; breeding males flush red-orange at the mouth and fins.
A streamlined native chub, once widespread but now essentially gone from the Grand Canyon reach, lost to dams and nonnative fish.
A small, tough introduced minnow that swarms warm shallows and competes with and preys on young native fish.
A hardy little nonnative minnow widely sold as bait; abundant in backwaters where it eats native fish eggs and larvae.
A big introduced bottom-feeder from Eurasia that roots up sediment and muddies backwaters, harming native habitat.
A large native sucker with thick, fleshy lips for scraping algae and insects off rocks; still common but declining basin-wide.
A native sucker with a cartilage-edged mouth for scraping algae from stones; the male's head flushes blue-green when spawning.
An endangered native sucker with a sharp keel behind its head; long-lived and now bolstered by hatchery-raised stockings.
A popular introduced sport fish thriving in the cold, clear tailwater below Glen Canyon Dam; also preys on young native fish.
An introduced European trout and a wary predator that takes native fish; targeted for removal to protect the humpback chub.
A large introduced, whiskered predator of warm reaches that hunts by smell at night and eats native fish.
A small introduced catfish of muddy backwaters, tolerant of warm, low-oxygen water.
A voracious introduced predator whose recent spread below the dam is a top threat to the humpback chub.
A small, aggressive introduced sunfish of warm sloughs that punches above its weight eating native fry.
A large introduced predator that moves up from downstream reservoirs and can eat sizable native fish.
A small, banded introduced fish of warm, shallow margins and backwaters.
The canyon's great cat — solitary, wide-ranging, and rarely seen; follows deer and bighorn through rough country.
A stub-tailed wildcat about twice house-cat size; an ambush hunter of rabbits and rodents, mostly seen at dawn and dusk.
The adaptable desert survivor whose yips echo off the walls at night; the clever trickster in countless Native stories.
A small fox that can climb trees, grizzled gray with a black-tipped tail, active mostly after dark.
A tiny, huge-eared fox of open desert flats that hunts by night and rarely needs to drink, taking water from its prey.
The familiar black-and-white skunk that ambles the river banks at night and warns before deploying its famous spray.
A small, agile skunk that does a warning handstand before spraying; a nimble climber and nocturnal hunter.
A powerful, low-slung digger with huge claws that excavates rodents and can vanish into the earth in minutes.
A wide-eyed, cat-sized relative of the raccoon nicknamed the 'miner's cat'; Arizona's state mammal, purely nocturnal and a superb climber.
The masked, ring-tailed bandit of streamsides; its dextrous paws probe water and camp gear alike.
The canyon's common deer, named for its big mule-like ears; browses green benches and bounds off in a stiff-legged 'stott.'
The canyon's icon of the cliffs — sure-footed rams with massive curled horns; a favorite subject of ancient petroglyphs.
A soft-gray chipmunk of rocky slopes and pinyon-juniper that dashes over boulders with its tail held high.
A large gray ground squirrel of the canyon's rocks and camps; bold, curious, and quick to raid unguarded food.
A small ground squirrel with a white side stripe that runs with its tail flipped over its back; active even in fierce heat.
A tiny, fur-lined-cheeked mouse of lava and rocks; desert forms evolve dark coats to match black rock.
A hopping, big-eyed rodent that never needs to drink — it makes water from dry seeds and bounds on huge hind feet.
A bipedal, long-tailed seed-hoarder of sandy ground that drums with its feet and lives on metabolic water.
The river's engineer; canyon beavers den in bank burrows rather than build lodges. Once trapped heavily along the Colorado.
A slow, quill-armored rodent that climbs trees to gnaw bark; its quills detach on contact but are not thrown.
A soft-furred, big-eared native mouse of rocky slopes and ledges, agile among the boulders at night.
The ubiquitous big-eyed native mouse and a key food for owls and snakes; a known hantavirus carrier, so keep food sealed.
A long-tailed native mouse of brushy, rocky slopes; a nimble climber in shrubs and rock piles.
A tiny native mouse that weaves a ball-shaped grass nest and feeds on seeds in grassy patches.
The desert 'packrat' that builds big stick middens among cactus and hauls off shiny objects; ancient middens preserve a record of past climate.
A stocky aquatic rodent with a rope-like tail that swims marshy backwaters feeding on cattails and reeds.
The small introduced mouse of Old World origin that travels with people and turns up around camps and gear.
A pale, big-eared rabbit of brushy flats that freezes then bolts in a zigzag; food for nearly every canyon predator.
A long-eared hare (not a rabbit) that sprints in great bounds; its huge ears shed heat in the desert sun.
The Southwest's smallest bat (formerly 'Western Pipistrelle'); a weak, fluttery flier out early at dusk over the water.
A bat with enormous rabbit-like ears; an agile, moth-hunting flier that roosts in caves and old mines.
A pale, big-eared bat that gleans scorpions and centipedes off the ground — and is immune to scorpion stings.
A robust, common bat that emerges at dusk to hawk beetles over water and camp.
A tiny mouse-eared bat with quick, erratic flight that forages low over the river for small insects.
A large, frost-tipped, tree-roosting bat that migrates long distances; a high, fast flier late in the evening.
A fast, high-flying bat with a tail extending past its membrane; famous for massive colonies and long foraging flights.
Descendants of prospectors' pack animals; tough desert survivors whose grazing and trampling damage springs and native plants, so they are managed as invasive.
A delicate fern of shaded seeps and dripping walls; its wiry black stems were prized for the black patterns in Indigenous basketry.
A large fern of permanent seeps and hanging gardens; a lush surprise in the desert where water never stops.
An ancient, jointed, leafless plant of wet banks; its gritty, silica-rich stems were used to scour pots, earning the name 'scouring rush.'
A jointed, leafless green shrub whose stems were long brewed into a tonic tea by Indigenous peoples and settlers, the source of the 'Mormon tea' name.
A gnarled, drought-hardy tree of the rims and slopes; its blue berry-like cones flavored food and medicine, and its shreddy bark and wood had countless uses.
The pinyon pine of the plateau; its rich, fatty pine nuts were and remain a treasured traditional food across the Southwest.
A rosette of stiff, spine-tipped leaves that blooms once on a tall stalk then dies; its roasted hearts were a staple food and its fibers made cordage and sandals.
A blue-gray agave of rocky slopes, roasted in stone pits for a sweet, nutritious food and a source of strong fiber.
Named for its fat, banana-like fruit that was roasted and eaten; the leaves gave fiber and the roots a natural soap.
A tree-like yucca whose roots ('amole') lather into soap and shampoo; its leaves split into cordage, sandals, and baskets.
A shaggy desert yucca with sharp leaves; a classic source of fiber for rope, mats, and sandals, with edible flowers and fruit.
The classic marsh plant; nearly every part is useful — starchy roots and pollen for food, fluff for insulation, leaves for mats and thatch.
A graceful bunchgrass whose plump seeds were a vital ground-into-meal food for desert peoples, especially in lean years.
A wispy native bunchgrass of sandy ground whose tiny seeds were gathered and ground for food.
A tall riverside cane (Phragmites) whose straight, hollow stems were made into arrow shafts, flutes, mats, and construction material.
A fine native bunchgrass named for the three bristly awns on each seed, which cling to fur and socks alike.
A giant ornamental plume-grass gone wild along the river; an aggressive invader that river crews pull out by hand at camps.
A fine invasive annual grass from Eurasia that cures to tinder and helps carry desert fires into places that rarely burned.
An invasive annual grass that greens up early then dries to fuel; its needle-sharp seeds work into socks and fur and drive destructive fire cycles.
A tough, spreading introduced lawn grass now naturalized on riverside sandbars and disturbed ground.
A native orchid of seeps and springs (also called chatterbox); its greenish, wine-veined flowers are a hidden treasure of wet canyon walls.
Not a cactus but a bundle of spiny, whip-like canes that leaf out after rain and flame with red flowers hummingbirds love; the canes were planted as living fences.
A broad-padded cactus whose fruits ('tunas') and young pads ('nopales') are traditional foods; the pads were also split as a cooling poultice.
Named for its round, flat, blue-green pads; it bears edible red fruit and hosts the cochineal insect once used for crimson dye.
A spineless-looking prickly pear (it has tiny barbed glochids instead) with vivid magenta blooms; its buds and fruit were eaten.
A mound-forming hedgehog cactus that lights up with brilliant scarlet, hummingbird-pollinated cups in spring; its fruit is edible.
A small clustering cactus with magenta flowers and sweet, strawberry-flavored fruit that was gathered as a treat.
A stout ribbed cactus that leans south (the 'compass cactus'); its curved spines made fishhooks and awls, but it is not a reliable water source.
A branching cholla with antler-like joints whose buds were pit-roasted as a calcium-rich food.
A fuzzy-looking but vicious cholla whose barbed joints detach at a touch — the notorious 'jumping cholla.' Handle with extreme care.
A small barrel-shaped cactus armored with hooked central spines that catch like fishhooks; it bears red fruit.
A native shrub or vine of shady side canyons with glossy leaves-of-three; its oil (urushiol) causes a nasty rash, so 'leaves of three, let it be.'
An aromatic three-leaflet shrub whose tart red berries make a lemonade-like drink; its straight young stems are a premier basketry material.
The signature evergreen shrub of the low desert, its resinous leaves giving off the smell of desert rain; a cornerstone of Indigenous medicine.
A tough streamside tree with net-veined leaves; its small orange berries are sweet and were gathered as food by people and wildlife alike.
A slender, thicket-forming willow; its flexible withes are a foundational basketry material for canyon tribes, and its bark holds a natural aspirin-like compound.
A large native tree willow that shades sandbars; its bark and withes were used for cordage, baskets, and medicine.
The great shade tree that marks water in the desert; Hopi carvers traditionally shape katsina (kachina) dolls from its soft root wood.
A dense, dark, thorny shrub that forms vast gray-black stands on desert benches; important winter browse for bighorn and deer.
An airy shrub with white rose-like flowers followed by feathery pinkish seed plumes; its twigs served as brooms and arrow shafts.
A fragrant cliff shrub (the 'quinine bush') whose shreddy bark was pounded into cordage, mats, sandals, and padding; prized browse for deer.
A thorny legume tree armed with hooked 'cat-claw' spines — the 'wait-a-minute bush'; its pods were ground into meal and its wood burned hot.
A spreading desert legume whose sweet pods were a dietary staple, ground into flour and fermented into drinks; the hard wood fueled fires and tools.
A thorny legume with showy pink pea-flowers; the blossoms were eaten and the wood was hard and durable.
A small tree that clouds pink-magenta before leafing out; its flowers are edible and its slender shoots are a valued red basketry element.
A deep-rooted, viciously spiny invasive legume from central Asia; it spreads along the river and is dug out by park crews at camps.
A silvery, thorny invasive tree from Eurasia that crowds out native willows and cottonwoods along the corridor and is targeted for removal.
A feathery pink-plumed invasive tree from Eurasia that guzzles water and salts the soil, choking native banks — now knocked back by an introduced leaf beetle.
A fast-growing, foul-smelling invasive tree that sprouts aggressively from its roots; crews watch for it moving into cleared tamarisk gaps.
A silvery-leaved plant topped with apricot-orange cups; its fine leaf hairs can irritate the eyes, earning the name 'sore-eye poppy.'
A tall native mustard with golden feathery plumes; it flags selenium-rich soil, and its greens were parboiled and eaten with care.
An aggressive invasive annual mustard that carpets disturbed ground and sandbars, crowding out native wildflowers; a top removal target at Lees Ferry.
A deep-rooted invasive mustard ('tall whitetop') that forms dense white-flowered stands and is very hard to eradicate once established.
A weedy invasive mustard that springs up in disturbed sandy soil after rain, with small yellow flowers and a peppery bite.
A silvery, salt-tolerant native shrub with papery four-winged seeds; its seeds were ground for food and its ashes used to color and enrich Hopi blue-corn dishes.
The classic tumbleweed — an invasive annual that dries, snaps off, and rolls, scattering seed; young shoots are edible but the mature plant is a spiny nuisance.
A low, sticky, sand-loving plant with fragrant pink flower clusters that scent the dunes, especially in the evening.
A native with magenta trumpet flowers that open in late afternoon; its deep starchy root was used medicinally in the Southwest.
A stemless plant whose big white blooms open at dusk and fade pink by morning, pollinated by night-flying hawkmoths.
A tall primrose with large lemon-yellow flowers that open in the evening and wilt by midday.
A sprawling plant with huge white moonflower trumpets that open at night; sacred and used ceremonially by some Southwestern peoples, but powerfully toxic and potentially deadly — admire, never touch.
A wild native tobacco with pale tubular flowers, smoked ceremonially by Indigenous peoples long before commercial tobacco.
A rangy invasive shrub from South America with tubular yellow flowers; despite the name it is highly toxic and must never be smoked or eaten.
A native streamside tree with velvety twigs that shades springs and side canyons and turns gold in autumn along the water.
Not a true willow but a catalpa relative with orchid-like pink trumpet flowers; its slender wood was used for bows and its flowers steeped as a tea.
A brilliant scarlet wildflower of dripping seeps and streambanks, its tubular blooms tailored to hummingbirds; the greens are edible.
A tall, fragrant penstemon with big pale-pink pouched flowers beloved by bees; a showy accent on rocky slopes.
A low penstemon that spangles the spring desert with vivid blue-to-lavender tubular flowers.
A spiny, thistle-like plant with crinkled white tissue-paper petals and yellow-orange sap; toxic, though the sap was applied traditionally to skin ailments.
A streamside tree of permanent water with small woody 'cones'; a marker of reliable springs and creeks deep in side canyons.
A large streamside tree with mottled white bark and huge maple-like leaves; a landmark of major side-canyon creeks.
A round desert shrub of silver leaves and golden daisies; its fragrant resin was burned as incense in Spanish missions and used as glue and salve.
A broom-like green shrub of washes and disturbed ground; in fall the females release clouds of silky, wind-borne seed.
A low, gray, much-branched shrub (bursage) that anchors vast stretches of desert flat and shelters the seedlings of larger plants.
A tall, straight-stemmed streamside shrub whose slender canes were bundled for arrow shafts, thatch, roasting racks, and cradleboards.
A willow-leaved shrub (not a true willow) that lines wet sandbars; its straight stems were used for construction, arrows, and simple tools.
A cheerful desert wildflower with long-lasting lemon-yellow daisies on silvery foliage; it blooms after rain in almost any season.
A toxic invasive from Eurasia with lavender thistle-like heads that poisons the soil against competitors; a serious rangeland pest.
A leafless parasitic tangle on mesquite and acacia; its sticky berries feed and are spread by the Phainopepla, though they are toxic to people.
A big-headed lizard with bold black neck-bands; males turn bright green-blue and can sprint upright on their hind legs.
A large, spotted, long-bodied lizard that ambushes insects and smaller lizards; gravid females flush orange.
A small, abundant lizard with a dark blotch behind each foreleg; the first lizard you'll see basking on almost any rock.
A slim, quick lizard of tree trunks, boulders, and canyon walls; males flash blue-green throat patches in display.
A spiny gray lizard whose males show flashy blue belly patches ('blue-bellies'); bobs and does 'push-ups' to signal.
A small spiny lizard of brushy, higher ground; males show blue throat and belly patches.
A large, rough-scaled lizard with black shoulder wedges; a bold basker that scampers up trees and rocks.
The flat, spiky 'horny toad' that eats ants and hunkers to match the sand; it can even squirt blood from its eyes to startle predators.
A rounded, short-spined horned lizard of higher elevations that gives live birth rather than laying eggs.
A big, potbellied plant-eating lizard that wedges into rock cracks and gulps air to swell up tight; long a traditional food.
A pale, heat-loving lizard active in the hottest hours that feeds heavily on creosote flowers and leaves.
A slender, striped, always-moving lizard that jerks along nosing under litter for insects.
A fast, striped-and-spotted whiptail of open desert, forever foraging with twitchy, restless movements.
An all-female species that reproduces by cloning — every individual is female and lays fertile eggs without males.
A soft-skinned, nocturnal little gecko with translucent banded skin that squeaks when caught and waves its tail like a cat.
One of only a few venomous lizards on Earth — a stout, beaded black-and-orange giant; rare in the far western canyon and fully protected. Leave it be.
A large, powerful constrictor that mimics a rattler when alarmed, hissing and buzzing its tail, but is completely harmless.
A long, fast, whip-thin snake (often a pinkish 'red racer' here) that hunts actively by day, racing down lizards in the heat.
A slender, speedy, striped snake with big eyes; a fast diurnal hunter of lizards and other snakes.
An agile, olive-striped racer that even climbs into shrubs after lizards and is quick to flee.
A glossy banded constrictor that famously eats other snakes — including rattlesnakes, whose venom it shrugs off.
A watchful streamside snake that hunts fish, tadpoles, and frogs in the shallows and dives readily when startled.
A handsome striped, water-loving snake of desert creeks and springs that forages for amphibians along the edges.
A small, secretive snake with vertical cat-like pupils, mildly venomous to its prey but harmless to people and active after dark.
A small dark snake with a bright neck ring and a vivid orange belly it curls up to flash as a warning.
A fast striped desert snake with an enlarged 'patch' scale on its snout used to dig out lizard eggs.
A gentle, banded burrowing snake with an upturned snout; nocturnal and harmless, sometimes mistaken for a coral snake.
A tiny, shiny, worm-like burrowing snake barely thicker than a noodle that lives underground eating ant and termite brood.
A pink-to-salmon rattlesnake found only in the canyon, its color tuned to the local rock; venomous — give it room and it will leave you alone.
A finely speckled rattler that blends perfectly with granite and limestone; venomous, and best simply avoided.
A mild-mannered rattler with a solid black tail; venomous but generally reluctant to strike.
The large, boldly diamond-patterned rattler with a black-and-white 'coon-tail'; venomous and defensive, so watch hands and feet at rest stops.
A blotched rattler of higher, cooler ground; venomous, and like all rattlers it would rather warn than bite.
A long-lived desert reptile that digs burrows and can live for decades; protected — never handle one, as a startled tortoise may empty its precious stored water.
A flat, leathery, pancake-shaped introduced turtle with a snorkel-like snout; a nonnative in the river that can deliver a quick bite.

indigenous: Twelve thousand years of people

People have lived in and around the Grand Canyon for at least 12,000 years, since Paleo-Indian hunters followed game across the plateaus at the end of the Ice Age. The canyon has never been empty wilderness — it is, and always has been, a homeland.
Split-twig figurines

In caves high in the Redwall limestone, archaeologists found tiny animal figures — deer and bighorn — folded from single split willow and cottonwood twigs, some 3,000 to 4,000 years old. Left by Archaic hunter-gatherers, likely as hunting offerings, they are among the oldest human traces in the canyon; Stanton’s Cave near Mile 32 held hundreds.
The Ancestral Puebloans and the river farms

From roughly AD 500 to 1200, Ancestral Puebloan people (once called ‘Anasazi’) farmed corn, beans, and squash on the river’s silt deltas — Unkar (Mile 72) and Nankoweap among them — and up on the rims. Thousands of sites remain: dwellings, granaries, roasting pits, check dams, and rock art.
The Nankoweap granaries

High in the cliff above Nankoweap (Mile 53), a row of stone-and-mud storage rooms built around AD 1100 still gazes out over the river — among the most evocative ruins in the canyon. Ancestral Puebloans stored grain there, safe from floods and rodents. Look and photograph, but never enter or touch.
Bright Angel Pueblo, at Phantom Ranch

Right where you’ll tie up boats at Phantom Ranch (Mile 88), just west of the Black Bridge, sits Bright Angel Pueblo — pit houses and a ceremonial kiva built by an extended Ancestral Puebloan family around AD 1050, at the mouth of Bright Angel Creek. Powell’s 1869 party camped on this beach and found the ruin. Wayside panels now interpret it; admire from the trail and don’t climb on the walls.
Agave roasting pits

Look for low rings or mounds of fire-cracked, blackened rock tucked near many camps and side canyons, more common through the western half of the canyon. These are agave roasting pits: agave hearts were piled on coals, covered with earth, and slow-roasted for days to convert the plant’s starches into something sweet and edible — a technique Pai and Paiute peoples still practice today.
The Cohonina and the Pai peoples
West of the Ancestral Puebloans lived the Cohonina, likely ancestors of today’s Pai peoples — the Havasupai and Hualapai — who have lived along the western canyon for many centuries.
The Hopi: place of emergence

For the Hopi, the Grand Canyon is sacred ground. Near the confluence of the Little Colorado River lies the Sipapuni, a golden travertine dome the Hopi hold as the place where their ancestors emerged into this world. The canyon and the Little Colorado remain central to Hopi religion today.
The Hopi salt pilgrimage

For generations, Hopi men made arduous pilgrimages to sacred salt deposits below the Little Colorado confluence, gathering salt and leaving offerings along a prescribed ceremonial route. The area is deeply sacred — the salt mines are closed to all visitors.
The Havasupai: people of the blue-green water

The Havasupai (‘people of the blue-green water’) are the only people who still live within the canyon, in Supai village deep in Havasu Canyon with its turquoise travertine waterfalls. For centuries they farmed the side canyon in summer and wintered on the rim — including the land that is now Grand Canyon Village.
Land taken — and returned

When the forest reserve and then the national park were created, the Havasupai were confined in 1882 to a tiny 518-acre reservation and pushed off their rim lands. After a decades-long fight, the Grand Canyon National Park Enlargement Act of 1975 returned about 185,000 acres to the Havasupai — one of the largest restorations of land to a tribe in U.S. history.
The Hualapai: people of the tall pines

The Hualapai hold the western South Rim and much of the river’s left bank from about Mile 165 to 274. Diamond Creek — the canyon’s only road down to the river, and your resupply point — sits on Hualapai land, as does Grand Canyon West. Camping and hiking river-left through their reach requires tribal permission.
Deer Creek: gateway to the spirit world

At Mile 136, a narrow slot canyon below Deer Creek Falls holds deep meaning for the Southern Paiute, who used this drainage for centuries: the slot is regarded as a passage for spirits moving from this life to the next. Some rock art panels in the area remain sacred to Southern Paiute people today. Enjoy the Patio above, but treat the narrows themselves with quiet respect and leave any rock art undisturbed and unphotographed.
Southern Paiute, Navajo, and Zuni

The Kaibab and San Juan Southern Paiute lived north of the river; the Navajo (Diné) hold the eastern rim and much of the Marble Canyon country; and the Zuni trace ancestral ties and pilgrimage routes into the canyon. In all, the National Park Service recognizes eleven traditionally associated tribes.
A living connection

These are not vanished cultures. The eleven associated tribes maintain deep spiritual, cultural, and physical ties to the canyon today and are increasingly partners in its care. As you travel, treat every ruin, spring, and salt deposit as someone’s church — because it is.
explore: In 1540, a Spanish party under García López de Cárdenas — sent by Coronado to chase rumors of golden cities — became the first Europeans to see the Grand Canyon, led to the South Rim by Hopi guides. Unable to find a way down to the river and short on water, they left, and Europeans largely ignored the canyon for two centuries.

In 1776, Franciscan priests passed through the region. Francisco Garcés visited the Havasupai in their canyon home, while the Domínguez–Escalante expedition, seeking a route to California, forded the Colorado upstream at a spot still called the Crossing of the Fathers — now beneath Lake Powell.

Lieutenant Joseph Ives steamed a boat up the lower Colorado in 1857–58 until it wrecked, then explored inland. His report dismissed the region as ‘altogether valueless’ and predicted the Grand Canyon would be ‘forever unvisited and undisturbed.’ History has rarely been so wrong.

John Wesley Powell was a self-taught geology professor and Union artillery officer who lost his right arm at Shiloh in 1862, the ball shattering it below the elbow. Undeterred, he spent the late 1860s exploring the Rockies, and in 1869 talked Congress into a small stipend and the Army into surplus rations for an expedition that professional explorers considered close to suicidal.

In May 1869, John Wesley Powell — a one-armed Civil War veteran — led ten men in four wooden boats from Green River, Wyoming, into country no map described. Three months later they became the first documented expedition to run the Grand Canyon, surveying and naming as they went. They nearly starved; boats splintered and food spoiled or washed away.

Near the end, exhausted and certain the next rapids were death, three men — William Dunn and the brothers Oramel and Seneca Howland — left the expedition at Separation Canyon (Mile 240) to climb out. They were never seen again, killed on the plateau above. Powell and the rest ran the rapids and reached safety two days later. The place still bears their leaving.
The second expedition, and the name

Powell returned in 1871–72 with a photographer and topographers, producing the first accurate maps and much of the canyon’s naming — it was Powell who popularized ‘Grand Canyon.’ He went on to found the U.S. Geological Survey and to warn, presciently, that the arid West held far less water than settlers hoped.

Powell went on to direct both the U.S. Geological Survey and the Smithsonian’s Bureau of Ethnology, channeling his canyon fame into decades of federal science and the documentation of Native American languages and cultures. He died in 1902; the canyon's main visitor viewpoint and a national forest bear his name today.
dams: In the 1880s and 90s, prospectors chased copper, silver, lead, and asbestos into the canyon, blasting and improving trails — many following ancient Indigenous routes. The Bright Angel Trail began as a Havasupai path widened by miners. Almost none of the claims paid.

The ore was mostly too poor and too remote to profit, and men like John Hance, William Bass, Seth Tanner, and Louis Boucher (‘the Hermit’) soon found that guiding and lodging visitors paid far better than digging — becoming the canyon’s first tourism entrepreneurs. Ralph Cameron ran the Bright Angel Trail as a private toll road and battled the Park Service for years.
The Orphan Mine and the guano folly

Uranium was pulled from the Orphan Mine on the South Rim into the 1960s, inside the park boundary. Across the western canyon, a company strung a mile-long aerial tramway in the 1950s to mine bat guano for fertilizer — a costly fiasco that ended after an Air Force jet clipped the cable.
Glen Canyon Dam changes the river

Completed just upstream in 1963, Glen Canyon Dam transformed the Colorado. The once-warm, silt-red, seasonally flooding river became cold, clear, and controlled, released from the bottom of Lake Powell. Native fish declined, sediment-starved beaches shrank, and the river you’ll run is, in a real sense, now a managed machine.
The dams that almost drowned the canyon

In the 1960s the Bureau of Reclamation proposed two more dams inside Grand Canyon itself — Marble Canyon Dam near Mile 39 and Bridge Canyon Dam in the west — to make power for the Central Arizona Project. Their reservoirs would have flooded long reaches of the river corridor you’re about to travel.
‘Should we also flood the Sistine Chapel?’

The Sierra Club, led by David Brower, fought back with full-page newspaper ads in 1966. To the claim that a reservoir would let tourists motor closer to the walls, one ad replied: ‘Should we also flood the Sistine Chapel so tourists can float nearer the ceiling?’ The IRS stripped the Club’s tax-exempt status the very next day — which only multiplied the public outrage.

Opposition was overwhelming. In 1968 Congress removed both Grand Canyon dams from the Central Arizona Project. It became one of the defining victories of the American environmental movement — the moment the country decided some places are worth more wild than dammed.

The Grand Canyon became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979. The Grand Canyon Protection Act of 1992 then required Glen Canyon Dam to be operated to protect downstream resources, leading to experimental ‘high-flow’ releases (from 1996 on) that deliberately flood the canyon to rebuild its sandbars and beaches — the very camps you’ll sleep on.
lore: In the 1890s, Utah trapper Nathaniel Galloway remade whitewater. Instead of rowing blindly forward, he faced downstream and pulled against the current to slow and steer — the ‘Galloway position’ that essentially every oarsman on the river still uses today.

Emery and Ellsworth Kolb, photographers whose studio clung to the South Rim, ran the river in 1911–12 hauling a movie camera. Their film — one of the first motion pictures of the canyon — played in their studio for decades; Emery narrated it in person until he died in 1976.

Honeymooners Glen and Bessie Hyde set out to run the canyon in a homemade wooden scow, Bessie hoping to become the first woman to do so. They vanished. Their boat was found weeks later, upright and fully loaded, gear untouched — but the couple was never found. It remains the canyon’s most enduring mystery.

Botanists Elzada Clover and Lois Jotter ran the entire canyon in 1938 with boatman Norman Nevills, becoming the first women known to complete the trip — cataloguing its plants along the way. Nevills went on to launch the canyon’s first commercial river trips.

In 1937 Buzz Holmstrom, a quiet Oregon gas-station attendant, ran the whole Colorado through the Grand Canyon alone, in a boat he built himself — the first known solo descent. Of the river itself, he wrote, ‘I have already had my reward.’

Georgie White Clark democratized the canyon. In the 1950s she lashed war-surplus pontoons into giant motorized ‘G-rigs’ that carried many passengers cheaply, and she ran trips into her 80s. Loud, fearless, and beloved, ‘Georgie’ put the river within reach of ordinary people.
Litton’s dories and the fight for the canyon

Martin Litton brought elegant, hard-hulled wooden dories to the Grand Canyon and never stopped fighting for it, a fierce voice against the dams. His dories — and their tradition of rowing rather than motoring — still run the river today.

River culture has its own lore. Rapids carry names from Powell and those after him — Sockdolager, Hance, Lava Falls — or from later runners, like Crystal, which grew monstrous after a 1966 flash flood. Even ‘the groover’ is history: named for the surplus ammo cans early boaters sat on, which pressed grooves into the seat.

rules.d: A permit is required for all noncommercial travel from Lees Ferry to Diamond Creek. The Trip Leader (permittee) named on the permit — or an approved Potential Alternate Trip Leader — must accompany the entire trip.

rules.t: Trip Leader is responsible for the party
rules.d: The Trip Leader must ensure every member follows these regulations plus all federal, state, local, and tribal laws. Violations can bring permit revocation, citations, and loss of future river access.
A copy of these regulations must be aboard and must be a current version — downloaded within 2 months of launch.

Everyone must be on the Participant List turned in at Lees Ferry and carry valid government photo ID with date of birth (driver license, state ID, or passport). No ID, no trip — except children 15 and under. Credit cards and birth certificates don’t count.
No one may take more than one river trip (commercial or noncommercial) per calendar year through any part of the Lees Ferry–Diamond Creek section.
Rangers may travel or camp with the trip and can ask to see the permit, passenger list, and Lees Ferry checkout sheet, and inspect camp procedures. Keep them handy.
Total participants — including the Trip Leader — may never exceed the permitted group size at any point in the trip.
People under one permit must travel and camp together on a single beach. You may split for a loop hike but must rejoin and camp together — and never split up to grab campsites ahead of other groups.

Sept 16–Mar 31 is non-motorized only — a launch in that window is oar/paddle power. Motor season is Apr 1–Sep 15. A non-motor trip may stow a motor for use only below Separation Canyon, with a signed waiver — never above Separation.
No vessel may travel primarily upstream above Separation Canyon (RM 240).

rules.t: Orientation & checkout: 3 PM the day before
rules.d: Everyone launching from Lees Ferry must attend the ranger orientation and checkout at 3:00 PM MST the day before launch (Arizona keeps no DST). Checkout is an inspection — expect gear to be opened to verify required equipment.

The Trip Leader checks in with the ramp ranger before unloading. With no ranger and no instructions, rigging may begin at noon up to one day before launch. Morning rigging (8:00–10:30 AM) is reserved for trips leaving that day.
Two vehicles per group on the ramp, only to unload, then move to the day lot. Overnight parking goes in the extended / 14-day lot — never on the ramp or day lot.

rules.t: River Runners Camp: one night, quiet hours
rules.d: The Private River Runners Camp is for the night before launch only (one-night limit, up to 16 people). Quiet hours 10 PM–6 AM MST. Carry out human waste and charcoal ash; no firewood gathering. After the trip, camp only in the Lees Ferry Campground.

Each PFD must be USCG-approved for whitewater/rafting/kayaking, Type I, III, or V, in good condition — no holes, tears, or broken/repaired buckles or zippers, and no patches on the main body. General boating, fishing, and ski vests aren’t allowed.
One per person, plus one spare per 10 people. Kayak/canoe trips add one spare per 4 boats.
Everyone must wear a properly fastened PFD at all times on the river at Separation Canyon (RM 240) and above. Below Separation, only children 12 and under are required to wear one (AZ law).
Each boat 16 ft and longer must carry a USCG-approved throwable flotation device in serviceable condition.

Each oar boat carries a spare set of oars; each paddle raft two spare paddles; kayak/canoe trips one spare paddle per 4 boats. Carry an air pump (for inflatables) and a patch/repair kit for every boat material on the trip.

A first aid kit on every boat. Emergency signaling: a USAF-type signal mirror and two 3×8-ft international-orange panels that form an ‘X’ visible from aircraft. A satellite phone or ground-to-air radio is strongly recommended (not required).
Every trip carries a gas stove (propane, white gas, etc.) with enough fuel for cooking. Charcoal may be used for cooking; wood fires are for warmth or ambiance only.

Wood/charcoal fires need a metal fire pan (≥ 300 sq in, 3-in lip on all sides) elevated on manufactured legs, over a fire blanket (~60×72 in, or ≥ 20% larger than the pan/Dutch oven). Pan & blanket are required on all trips launching Nov 1–end of Feb, and any time you burn wood or charcoal.

Nov 1–end of Feb you may burn beach driftwood; the rest of the year all wood must be packed in. Never pre-collect wood for later, and never gather from standing or fallen trees. Fires only on river-corridor beaches.
All ash and fire residue must be carried out of the canyon.

rules.t: Carry out all solid waste + TP
rules.d: All solid human waste and toilet paper must leave the canyon. In camp use the washable, reusable, park-approved toilet; between camps and on day hikes use a wag-bag (PETT/Restop) system. Plastic ‘Scat Packer’ buckets are prohibited.

rules.t: Pack out feces from side hikes
rules.d: When hiking away from camp, bag all feces and carry it back to camp. Put toilet paper in the main toilet — never burn it.

Urinate directly into the Colorado in the main corridor, or into your toilet. At night use the trip’s pee bucket and pour it into the river in the morning. Away from the river, go ‘high and far’ — at least 100 ft from trails, camps, and side streams.

Cans, rubbish, and refuse may never be left in the water, on shore, or in side canyons — carry it all out. No trash deposits at Phantom Ranch, Diamond Creek, Pearce Ferry, or South Cove. Strain liquid garbage through fine mesh; crush cans on a tarp or below the high-water line.
Place tarps under food prep, serving tables, and the dishwashing station to keep food scraps off the beach.
Use soap only in the main Colorado, never in side streams or within 100 yards of a side-stream junction. Solar showers must be used standing in the main flow.

Wash hands after the toilet and after handling raw meat before touching other food. Sanitize prep surfaces and utensils with a 100–200 ppm chlorine solution; keep raw-meat gear separate until cleaned.
Cook meat and poultry to 165°F. Keep cold foods below 45°F and hot foods above 140°F. Reheat leftovers to 165°F (best saved for emergencies).
Wash below the high-water line: pre-wash, wash (120–140°F soapy), dip-rinse, then sanitize 60 seconds in a 50–100 ppm chlorine bath; air-dry on a rack.

Treat all drinking and cooking water: a rolling boil for 1 minute, or filter to ≤ 0.2 microns plus a disinfectant (≈ 2 drops chlorine per gallon). Settle muddy water overnight or with alum (1 tsp per 5 gal) and decant before treating. Draw from the mainstem unless it’s very silty.
Any gastrointestinal illness must be logged on the Confidential Illness Report Form. If 3+ people fall ill, notify NPS Dispatch (928-638-7805) within 24 hours by sat phone.

Set camp on resilient post-dam sandbars within 100 yards of the water line. Don’t trample vegetation or blaze new routes or sleeping areas in the fragile desert zone. Stay on established trails and avoid shortcutting.

No camping at: Paria confluence–Navajo Bridge (RM 0.8–4.5), Little Colorado confluence area (RM 60.9–65.5), within 100 yds of Shinumo (RM 109.2), within ¼ mi of Elves Chasm (RM 117.2), Deer Creek (RM 136.6–137.4), and Havasu (RM 157.2–157.8). Day-use only (no camping): Tapeats (RM 134.3), Kanab (RM 144), Matkatamiba (RM 148.4). Redwall Cavern (RM 33.3): no camping and no fires.

From RM 77.5 (below Hance) to RM 89.8 (below Pipe Creek), Mar 1–Oct 31 these are Phantom Exchange Camps (exchange trips only) with no layovers. Outside those dates (Nov 1–Feb 28/29) trips have more latitude, but there’s no camping right around Phantom Ranch except the Pipe Creek camp (RM 89.2) or emergencies approved by the Phantom ranger.
Camping is limited to the three marked camps (First, Main, Lower), one party each. Hikers must disembark only at those camps or the mouth of Nankoweap Creek.

No entry: Anasazi Bridge (RM 43.3), Hopi Salt Mines (RM 63.5–65), Furnace Flats (RM 71.5–72.2), Hance & Bass mines (asbestos), Bat Cave (RM 266.8), Rampart Cave (RM 274.5). No camping within 300 yds of Columbine Falls (RM 274.9).

River-left above the historic high-water line from RM 165–274 is Hualapai Tribal Land — camping or hiking there needs Hualapai approval. Hiking up Havasu past the Beaver Creek confluence requires Havasupai fees/permits.
Don’t remove or disturb rocks, fossils, plants, mining artifacts, or Indigenous artifacts (36 CFR 2.1).
No cats, dogs, or other pets on the trip.
Generators only for emergencies and inflating rafts — not for lights, appliances, or sound. Boats running at night must show USCG running lights.

Quagga mussels are present in the river and Lake Mead. Clean, Drain, and Dry all boats and gear at the trip’s end and before launching on any new water, then wait at least 5 days before entering another waterway.
Only the NPS arranges helicopter evacuations, and only for medical emergencies. Evacuation costs are the patient’s responsibility.

Emergency number: (928) 638-7911. By radio, give your LOCATION (river mile), then CRITICAL or STABLE, TRAUMA or MEDICAL, and PRIVATE or COMMERCIAL trip. A sat phone is most reliable; a signal-mirror flash is often the best way to reach aircraft.

Pick a level ~15×15-ft spot clear of obstacles for 75 ft; set the orange ‘X’ near (not on) it; gather everyone 100+ ft away with loose gear secured; wet the pad down; never approach the helicopter unless the crew signals, and never from the rear.

Report any evacuation, injury needing more than first aid, death or disappearance, or property damage over $500. File the Incident Report Form within 7 days (or within 24 hours if another agency ran a serious/hospitalization evac). Carry the forms on the trip.

The Pearce Ferry ramp is take-out only — no launching, swimming, camping, or shoreline fires. Keep the ramp clear and de-rig in the spaces up- or down-stream. Scout Pearce Ferry Rapid (½ mile below the South Cove option), which many rate the hardest in the canyon, before deciding to run it.
River recreation fees are paid online before the permit issues. Diamond Creek takeouts owe additional Hualapai Tribe fees (per person, boat, and vehicle), arranged in advance.

rules.t: Leave No Trace: walk only on durable surfaces
rules.d: Stay on rock, established trails, sandbars, and streambeds — never on undisturbed desert. That dark, knobby crust between the plants is cryptobiotic soil: a living skin of moss, lichen, and bacteria that holds the sand together and feeds the desert. A single boot print can take decades to heal, so rock-hop, follow washes, and walk single-file on trails that already exist.

rules.t: Pee in the river, not on the beach
rules.d: Dilution is the solution — urinate into the wet sand at the water’s edge or straight into the current. Urine left on dry sand and rock concentrates as it evaporates, reeks in the sun, and draws animals to dig at the salt. At night use the trip pee bucket and empty it into the river in the morning.

The groover is for solid waste only. Urine turns it into a heavy, sloshing, foul mess that’s miserable to haul and to clean at the takeout. Keep the two separate — river or pee bucket for liquid, every time.

Potsherds, ruins, rock art, fossils, and wildflowers all stay exactly where they are — for the law (36 CFR) and for the next boat down. Take photos, stack no cairns, build nothing, and leave every camp looking wild.

rules.t: Keep it quiet and share the canyon
rules.d: Sound carries for miles off the walls. Keep voices and music low, especially after dark; give other groups room at camps and attractions; and let the river’s own soundtrack be the loudest thing most of the time.

rules.t: Ride the tailwaves out of rapids
rules.d: The fastest water runs down the tongue and through the tailwaves in the main channel. Punch through and stay center rather than drifting to the edges — catch an eddy and you’ll spin, stall, and burn real time and muscle rowing back out into the current.

rules.t: Fireline the boats before tents go up
rules.d: When the whole group forms a line and passes every bag ashore — personal and group gear alike — before anyone pitches a tent, camp sets up dramatically faster. No boat sits half-unloaded, and the kitchen crew can start while others make camp.

rules.t: Stage the fire, but hold the match
rules.d: Build the fire pan and lay the fire ready to go, then wait. If it’s warm, still light out, bug-free, and folks haven’t gathered around yet, you may not need one at all — saving wood, ash to pack out, and the whole burn-down at the end of the night.

rules.t: Know the ‘tides’ and ride the high water
rules.d: The river isn’t tidal — it rises and falls each day as Glen Canyon Dam ramps its releases (hydropeaking). Higher flows give more push and bury rocks; low water is slower and bonier. Time big-mileage days and rocky, technical stretches for the higher, faster water when you can.

rules.t: Know the dinner plan; pull only what you’ll use
rules.d: Keep each night’s menu in mind so you unload only the food and gear you’ll actually use that evening instead of excavating and re-stowing the whole boat. Camp goes faster, the beach stays tidy, and the coolers stay cold and packed.

landmarks.name: Lees Ferry Boat Ramp
landmarks.desc: Mile 0 — the launch point for virtually every Grand Canyon river trip. The journey downstream begins here.

landmarks.name: Phantom Ranch - Water Refill
landmarks.desc: The only developed outpost deep in the canyon, at the foot of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails — a vital water and refill stop.

landmarks.name: Diamond Creek Boat Ramp
landmarks.desc: The only road-accessible point on the river inside the canyon (on Hualapai land) — a very common take-out.

landmarks.name: Pearce Ferry Boat Ramp
landmarks.desc: The final take-out, where the moving river gives way to the still water of Lake Mead.
